summary: Describes a mechanism for LISP in which each endpoint-to-locator mapping carries a version number, sent in the LISP header of encapsulated packets. This helps routers notice when their mapping is out of date. It was replaced by RFC 9302.

eli5.summary: Every address-book page has a number on it. When a letter shows a newer number, you know your page is old and you should fetch the new one.

questions: how does lisp detect stale mappings
how are version numbers encoded in lisp headers
subtitle: Detect stale mappings in LISP by embedding version numbers in packets

tldr.problem: In LISP, routers cache EID-to-RLOC mappings to know where to send packets. When a mapping changes, cached copies become stale, but routers don't know until they send a packet and it fails.
tldr.mechanism: Assign a version number to each EID-to-RLOC mapping and embed both source and destination version numbers in the LISP header of encapsulated packets. Receiving routers compare versions against their cache to detect stale information.
tldr.outcome: Routers can proactively detect stale mappings and request updates without disrupting traffic, improving convergence in LISP networks, though this experimental approach was later updated in RFC 9302.

today: RFC 6834 is an Experimental RFC that was obsoleted by RFC 9302, which provides an updated map-versioning specification for LISP.

sections.title: The Problem of Stale Mappings
sections.content: The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) separates endpoint identifiers (EIDs, like IP addresses) from routing locators (RLOCs, the actual forwarding addresses). To encapsulate a packet, an Ingress Tunnel Router (ITR) looks up the destination EID in a cache of EID-to-RLOC mappings that were learned from Map-Reply messages. If the mapping changes at the authoritative Egress Tunnel Router (ETR), the cached copy becomes stale. The ITR might continue using the old RLOC, sending packets to the wrong place. Without a mechanism to detect this, stale mappings cause traffic loss until the cache entry naturally expires. Map-Versioning adds version numbers to mappings, allowing receivers to detect when mappings are out of date.
sections.eli5: Routers store notes about where to send packets. If those notes change at the source, the router might still have the old note and send packets to the wrong place. Version numbers let the router notice the note is old before traffic breaks.

sections.title: Map-Version Numbers and Circular Ordering
sections.content: Each EID-to-RLOC mapping is assigned a unique Map-Version number, an unsigned 12-bit integer from 1 to 4095. (The value 0 is reserved as the Null Map-Version, indicating that versioning is not used for that mapping.) When a mapping changes—by adding or removing RLOCs, or by changing their priorities or weights—the version number is incremented to identify the new version. Version numbers use circular ordering, meaning that half of the version number space is considered newer and half is older relative to the current version. For example, with version 69, version numbers 70 through 2117 are newer, while 2118 through 68 (wrapping around) are older. This circular ordering allows version numbers to wrap around without confusion about whether a number is newer or older.
sections.eli5: Each address book has a number on it. When the book changes, the number goes up. But the numbers are arranged in a circle, so 4095 wraps back to 1, and you have to be smart about which direction is "newer."

sections.title: Detecting Stale Mappings in Received Packets
sections.content: When an ETR receives a LISP-encapsulated packet, it checks the version numbers in the LISP header. Each packet carries two version numbers: a Destination Map-Version (for the destination EID's mapping) and a Source Map-Version (for the source EID's mapping). The ETR compares these against its own EID-to-RLOC database and cache. If the Destination Map-Version is older than the ETR's current version, the packet's sender (ITR) has a stale mapping. The ETR can then send a Map-Request to inform the ITR of the newer mapping. If the Source Map-Version is newer than what the ETR has cached, the ETR's cache is stale and it should request an update. If a packet arrives with a version number that is newer than what the authoritative ETR has, the packet is invalid (someone is spoofing or misbehaving) and SHOULD be dropped.
sections.eli5: When a packet arrives, the router checks its version numbers. If they are older than what the router knows, the sender is using old information. If they are newer, something is wrong. If they match, everything is fine.

sections.title: Encoding Version Numbers in LISP Headers
sections.content: Version numbers are carried in the LISP-specific header of encapsulated packets. When the V-bit (version bit) in the LISP header flags is set to 1, the low-order 24 bits of the first longword (four octets) of the LISP header are interpreted as two 12-bit version numbers: the first 12 bits hold the Source Map-Version number, and the second 12 bits hold the Destination Map-Version number. When the V-bit is 0, these bits are used for other LISP functions and version numbers are not present. The mechanism is transparent to routers that do not support versioning; they simply ignore the V-bit and these 24 bits. Additionally, Map Records in Map-Request, Map-Reply, and Map-Register messages carry a 12-bit Map-Version field before the EID-Prefix-AFI field, indicating the version of the mapping being announced.
sections.eli5: Version numbers are packed into the packet header where there is space for them. Older routers ignore them safely because they use different bits. The version is also announced in the control messages that say "here is a new mapping."

sections.title: Benefits and Practical Applications
sections.content: Map-Versioning improves LISP convergence in several scenarios. When a mapping changes, ETRs can immediately detect that incoming packets use old versions and notify ITRs to refresh their caches, avoiding prolonged traffic loss. It helps with graceful RLOC shutdown: when taking a RLOC offline, an ETR increments the version number while marking the RLOC as unreachable, allowing all active senders to discover the change before the RLOC actually goes down. In unidirectional traffic (where the ETR has no cache entry for the source), the Source Map-Version is simply ignored, making the mechanism compatible with asymmetric flows. Map-Versioning also works with LISP interworking features like Proxy-ITRs and Proxy-ETRs, which can use the Null Map-Version value when they do not have a mapping to announce. The mechanism enables lighter-weight LISP implementations that do not need to track Locator-Status-Bits independently.
sections.eli5: Version numbers help routers notice mapping changes quickly instead of waiting for the cache to expire. It works even when traffic only flows one way, and it helps during maintenance when a location shuts down.
